paper_title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: In standard language model, model size and computation grow together because almost every weight takes part in processing every token [13]. N-gram embedding tables separate the two by adding large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens. At each position, the model looks up vectors for the short sequences ending at the current token, such as the two-token bigram and three-token trigram. Because far too many such sequences exist to give each its own row, fixed hash function maps each sequence to row of the table [4, 5]. Each position reads only few rows however large the tables are, so their size is decoupled from the computation each token costs, and the tables can hold billions of parameters at little computational cost. Earlier models placed n-gram embedding tables only at the input [6, 7], whereas recent designs place them inside the network so that looked-up vectors interact with intermediate representations. DeepSeeks Engram inserts hashed n-gram tables into selected layers and gates the retrieved vectors with the layers hidden state [8]. Follow-up designs change how each table is structured: TN-gram shares tensor factors across ngram orders [9], FactorEngram stores sparse coefficients over learned dictionary [10], and X-gram allocates rows by token frequency [11]. Despite these differences, these methods commonly use separate n-gram embedding table for each layer (Figure 2a). Separate tables are costly in memory: reading n-grams at more layers either multiplies table size or leaves fewer rows per table and more hash collisions. They also prevent layers from sharing what they learn about the same token sequences. This work extends human-verified finding made by an rStation agent (https://rstation.ai/) as part of our Autonomous Research Program (https://dualverse.ai/auto_research). Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation Figure 1: Scaling curves with respect to table size. ClimbMix, nine-layer model (20.7M backbone), ten table sizes. Validation bits per byte (lower is better) against table size. Curves show Chorus, Engram and FactorEngram; isolated points show OE, TN-gram and two X-gram configurations. One seed per point. Sharing single table across layers is the natural alternative, and simple forms of it exist. Compact training recipes add token-indexed vectors to the attention values of several layers [12, 13]. single hashed bigram table has likewise been shared across layers [12, 14]. Sharing single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. Early and late layers perform different computations, so fixed vector suited to one depth need not suit another. We therefore ask whether one set of n-gram embedding tables can let each layer read what it needs, and how such design compares empirically with separate tables for each layer. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way (Figure 2b). In Chorus, n-gram embeddings and token embedding are combined and refined to obtain one refined embedding for the whole network. Each layer that uses this vector first adapts it to its own needs: it rescales the components of the vector by factors computed from its current hidden state, and then maps the result through its own projection layer. The rescaling lets layer emphasize the components of the refined embedding that matter in its current context, and the projection maps them into the form that layers own computation uses, so the same refined embedding can serve an early layer and late one differently. We compare Chorus with existing n-gram methods on nine-layer model with 20.7M backbone parameters, GPT-style model from the nanochat codebase [13], trained on ClimbMix [15] with ten table sizes from 20M to 9.6B (Figure 1). Chorus reaches lower validation loss than Engram and FactorEngram at every table size tested. The margin is large: with 1.2B tables, Chorus predicts text better than either baseline does with 9.6B, so it surpasses their best quality with 87% smaller tables. The result carries over to another dataset. On FineWeb [16], with nine-layer model of 17.1M backbone parameters, Chorus reaches 1.193 bits per byte against 1.198 for TN-gram, the strongest of four baselines. It also generalizes to larger network: in an 18-layer model with 133M backbone parameters, Chorus reaches 1.057 bits per byte against 1.066 for Engram and 1.065 for TN-gram. We further show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. Our contributions are as follows: design for sharing n-gram tables across the network. Chorus combines per-token table and hashed n-gram tables into one vector used at the input and in the attention values of every other layer, where each layer rescales it from its hidden state and applies its own projection. (a) Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram keep separate n-gram table for every place that reads one, including the input. (b) Chorus looks up one set of tables once and reuses the result at the input and in every other layer. Each layer rescales the refined embedding using its own hidden state (dashed arrows) and maps it through its own projection. Lower loss at every table size, and the same quality with 87% smaller tables. Across ten table sizes from 20M to 9.6B on ClimbMix, Chorus achieves lower validation loss than Engram and FactorEngram at every size and outperforms their 9.6B models using 1.2B tables. The advantage holds across datasets and at larger scale. Chorus has the lowest loss among seven methods on ClimbMix, outperforms four baselines on FineWeb, and improves over Engram and TN-gram in an 18-layer, 133M-parameter model. Memory-efficient training with Ember. Training Choruss tables with Ember saves 99.2% of their optimizer-state memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance.

Training the tables. To reduce optimizer memory, we propose training the tables with Ember [18], recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer previously applied to token-indexed tables; here, we apply it to hashed n-gram tables. Instead of keeping two moment arrays with the same shape as the table, as in AdamW, Ember stores only one scalar per row and one per column by factoring the second-moment estimate and omitting momentum. Concretely, Ember computes bias-corrected exponential averages ˆri and ˆc of the mean squared gradient in each row and each column, using decay β = 0.95. Denoting by any of the tables U, E1, . . . , E4, and by its gradient, each row accessed in the batch is updated as E[i] E[i] η G[i] pˆri ˆc/ mean(ˆc) + ϵ . (5) Here η is the learning rate and ϵ numerical stabilizer. Note that the hidden-layer weight matrices still use Muon [19, 20], instead of Ember. For each table, Ember reduces optimizer-state storage from 2RC values with typical optimizer such as AdamW to + values. At table size of 1.2B, Ember therefore reduces the table-optimizer state from 4.47 GiB to 35.7 MiB, about 128 less  (Table 2)  .

sections.title: 3 Results
sections.content: We evaluate GPT-style autoregressive Transformers, using nanochat-based [13] nine-layer, 20.7M-parameter model on ClimbMix [15], and Parameter Golf models with nine layers (17.1M parameters) or 18 layers (133M parameters) on FineWeb [16]. Within each setting, methods share the backbone initialization and data order, and are trained on 3.15B tokens for the nine-layer models or 5.24B tokens for the 18-layer models. We compare with plain model, OE [6], X-gram [11], Engram [8], TN-gram [9] and FactorEngram [10]. Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram use the optimizers suggested in their papers. To ensure fair comparison based on the actual number of added parameters, we count the token and ngram tables together with all other learnable parameters introduced by Chorus (e.g., the per-layer projection weights). Since the embedding tables account for most of these parameters, we call this total number of parameters the table size. We report validation bits per byte, with lower values indicating better prediction. Method-comparison tables use three seeds and report means and standard errors; the size curve, component ablations and order sweep use one seed. More experimental details can be found in Section A. 5 Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation Figure 3: Training curves at two model sizes. FineWeb. (a) Nine-layer model (17.1M backbone), 26M tables. (b) 18-layer model (133M backbone), 60M tables. Plain model means no added n-gram tables. Both panels show validation bits per byte on fixed 2,048-sequence subset during training, mean standard error over three seeds. Final full-validation results are in Table 1.

sections.title: 3.1 Evaluation Results
sections.content: To understand how Chorus scales with memory size, we train the nine-layer model on ClimbMix with Chorus, Engram, and FactorEngram at ten table sizes ranging from 20M to 9.6B. We increase table size by increasing row counts while holding each embedding width fixed. The scaling results are shown in Figure 1. Chorus achieves the lowest validation loss at every table size; at 9.6B, it reaches 0.9148 BPB, compared with 0.9258 for FactorEngram and 0.9273 for Engram. Increasing the table size from 4.8B to 9.6B reduces the loss by further 0.0039 BPB, suggesting that Chorus could benefit from even larger tables. Notably, with only 1.2B tables, Chorus achieves 0.9229 BPB, outperforming all 9.6B baselines with 87% smaller tables, demonstrating its memory efficiency. Comparisons across settings with multiple seeds show the same advantage  (Table 1)  . Beyond ClimbMix, we test FineWeb using similar nine-layer model, where Chorus again achieves the lowest validation loss on every seed. We also evaluate the models using larger 133M-parameter 18-layer backbone with 60M tables; Chorus achieves the lowest validation loss on every seed against the tested baselines. Training curves show that Chorus leads at four of five recorded checkpoints for the nine-layer model, with the sole exception being the first evaluation at update 1000, where TN-gram performs slightly better (Figure 3). For the 18-layer model, Chorus leads at all nine recorded checkpoints. These results indicate that the performance benefit carries across datasets and model sizes. Beyond validation loss on pretraining data, we evaluate the effect of Chorus on downstream tasks by applying trained 18-layer models to 22 tasks from the DCLM evaluation collection [13, 21]. Across the full suite of 22 tasks, Chorus achieves the highest mean score of 0.1240 0.0016, about 0.0030 ahead of TN-gram, the strongest baseline (Figure 4). These gains are particularly pronounced on Wikidata question answering, where Chorus reaches 25.84 2.74% accuracy compared to 17.38 1.20% for Engram and 18.57 1.28% for TN-gram, demonstrating improvements in entity factual recall. We also see improvements on LAMBADA, CoQA, and HellaSwag, which are more closely related to natural-language prediction and comprehension. Chorus has slightly lower accuracy than the baselines on CommonsenseQA and Dyck languages, which are more related to reasoning capability, but neither difference is statistically significant across the three seeds. This pattern suggests that Chorus may help more with factual recall and contextual prediction, likely due to better phrase association. Further downstream evaluation of the smaller model is discussed in Section B.2. 6 Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation Figure 4: Downstream accuracy. FineWeb, 18-layer model (133M backbone), 60M tables. Plain model means no added n-gram tables. Accuracy of Chorus minus that of each baseline on 22 tasks and on their average, in percentage points; mean standard error of paired differences over three seeds. Table 2: GPU optimizer memory saved by Ember. ClimbMix, nine-layer model (20.7M backbone). The state memory is computed using the conventional storage precision for each optimizer.

sections.title: 3.2 Optimizer Choice
sections.content: We use Ember instead of conventional AdamW to train n-gram embeddings because it reduces optimizerstate memory during training. Since optimizer states are typically stored on the GPU, this saving allows larger tables to fit on the same GPU. At table size of 1.2B, Ember requires 35.7 MiB of state compared with 4.47 GiB for AdamW, saving 4.44 GiB (99.2%; Table 2). Beyond memory savings, we examine how optimizer choice affects different n-gram methods. We train Chorus, Engram, FactorEngram, and simpler shared-bigram design with both AdamW and Ember at table size of 76M, using three seeds per combination  (Table 3)  . Ember slightly improves performance for Chorus, Engram, and the shared-bigram design, but substantially worsens performance for FactorEngram. This suggests that its benefit does not extend to all n-gram methods.

sections.content: We perform ablation analysis on Chorus to understand the importance of each component, as shown in Figure 5. Components also used in previous work and baselines are important. For example, the token table has the largest effect: removing it increases validation loss from 0.9469 to 0.9634 BPB, even when its parameters are reallocated to the n-gram tables. possible explanation is that dedicated token rows complement the context-dependent phrase features with memory of individual tokens. Removing either read increases loss significantly, showing that the refined embedding provides useful information at both stages of the model. Splitting the input and layer lookup tables into separate pools also hurts performance. After splitting, each pool gets only half the table size to keep the total table size fixed, which is less efficient than reusing the same table at full size. This suggests that the n-gram tables for the input and intermediate-layer attention contain knowledge that can be shared and reused. Layer-specific projection is also important: sharing single projection across all layers substantially increases validation loss, indicating that layer-specific adaptation is needed for knowledge reuse. The other design choices mostly provide modest gains. For example, rescaling by the channel gate sℓ and input gate bt improves performance moderately, while gate at shows no benefit in this comparison. This may reflect overlapping gate functions that make at redundant in this setting. Longest n-gram order. sections.title: 4 Related work
sections.content: Token and n-gram embedding tables. Tensor factors [9], sparse dictionaries [10], and frequency-based allocation [11] improve embedding-table efficiency by changing how entries are represented or allocated within table. These approaches focus on how entries are represented and allocated within table. In contrast, Chorus focuses on sharing the same n-gram table throughout the model to save memory and reuse knowledge, complementing such table designs. Recent work also shows that n-gram tables can be stored in low precision to save memory at inference, but not during training [22]. Sharing embeddings across layers. Compact training recipes add token-indexed embeddings to attention values [12, 13]. MoME uses context gate to select among multiple vectors per token and also evaluates sharing its token table across memory layers [14]. Memory Attention constructs values by combining layer-specific token memories with contextual keys [23]. Value Residual Learning instead reuses contextual attention values: ResFormer carries first-layer values to deeper layers through residual connections, and 9 Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation SVFormer shares them across all layers [24]. However, these works study different settings from ours, which is n-gram embedding sharing during pre-training. Optimizers for large tables. We use Ember [18] to train our shared embedding tables. Previous n-gram methods commonly use Adam or AdamW [811]. Ember was originally evaluated on input embeddings and language-model output weights, with additional tests on token-indexed value tables. We apply it to hashed n-gram tables and show that it reduces optimizer memory while preserving predictive performance in Chorus and some other n-gram embedding methods.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we propose Chorus, an n-gram embedding method that shares tables across the input and intermediate layers while adapting to each layers needs. Empirical results show improvements over existing baselines across model sizes and training datasets. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.

sections.title: A Experiment Details
sections.content: A.1 Models, data and training We use nanochat-based model on ClimbMix and the Parameter Golf model family on FineWeb, following the setting used by TN-gram [9, 13, 15, 16]. The main model sizes and training budgets are listed in Table 4. ClimbMix uses an 8,192-token byte-pair vocabulary; FineWeb uses the public tokenized data and 1,024-token SentencePiece vocabulary from Parameter Golf. The models use 1,024-token context and grouped-query attention with eight query heads and four key/value heads. Table 4: Model and training settings. Backbone and table sizes are in millions or billions of parameters. Method comparisons use three seeds; the scaling curve uses one seed at each size. ClimbMix FineWeb, small FineWeb, large Layers / width Backbone parameters Vocabulary size Training tokens Table size 9 / 512 20.71M 8,192 3.15B 20M9.6B 9 / 512 17.06M 1,024 3.15B 26M 18 / 1,024 133.25M 1,024 5.24B 60M Methods within each setting share the same backbone initialization, data order and training budget. Each update processes 524,288 prediction targets, giving 6,000 updates for the nine-layer models and 10,000 for the 18-layer models. Learning rates remain constant for the first 80% of training and then decay linearly to zero. The models original token-indexed value tables are removed in all comparisons. Intermediate training curves use fixed validation subset; final BPB uses the full validation split. All experiments use RTX 5090 GPUs. Initialization. The token and n-gram tables and the convolution are initialized to zero, so the added memory initially contributes zero to the model. The input projection Win starts as the identity, and each layer projection Pℓ starts as one quarter of rectangular identity. The layer gates Aℓ and Gℓ start at zero, giving initial rescaling factors of one; the local-context map Wc uses small uniform initialization. All these maps and the depthwise convolution are bias-free. Major optimizer settings. We retain the backbone training recipe: Muon with learning rate 0.04 for matrices, Adam with 0.05 for embeddings, and Adam with 0.04 for the remaining backbone parameters. Chorus tables use Ember with learning rate 0.2(d/768)1/2, second-moment decay 0.95 and no weight decay. Its projection and gate matrices use Muon with weight decay decaying from 0.2 to zero, and its convolution uses AdamW with learning rate 0.04. A.2 Baseline configurations We adapt the baselines from their papers or released implementations, retaining their main design and table optimizer. Table row counts or factor ranks are adjusted to the table sizes used in each comparison. Layer numbers below use zero-based indexing. Engram. Engram inserts hashed n-gram memories at selected layers [8]. On ClimbMix, we use bigrams and trigrams after layers 1 and 4; on FineWeb, we use orders 25 after layers 1 and 7. Table sizes are chosen as consecutive primes, lookup uses the models token vocabulary, and table and other memory parameters use AdamW with learning rates 0.05 and 0.04, respectively. TN-gram. TN-gram uses factorized n-gram memories at selected layers [9]. We use orders 25 after layers 1 and 7. Factor ranks are 848 on ClimbMix at 76M parameters and 1,409 on nine-layer FineWeb at 26M. The 18-layer result uses factor rank of 2,252 to match the 60M table size. Factors use AdamW with learning rate 0.05, and key/value projections use Muon. 13 Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation FactorEngram. FactorEngram represents n-gram memories with sparse coefficients over shared dictionary [10]. We use its unigram, bigram and trigram tables before layers 3 and 4, with four heads per order, width 3d and sparsity penalty 103. Table and other memory parameters use AdamW with learning rates 0.001 and 0.01, respectively. X-gram and OE. X-grams routing tables are built from token frequencies in our training data [11]. We use the released configuration with two value-stream views per layer; its larger scaling-curve point additionally uses three hidden-stream views. OE adds four hashed bigram and trigram tables to the input embedding, using the full table budget and Ember for table updates [6].

sections.content: B.1 Scaling with table size Table 5 gives the full results behind the scaling curves in Figure 1. In these runs, Chorus uses Ember, while Engram and FactorEngram use AdamW. For table sizes above 2.4B parameters, we use more than one GPU because of the memory limits of our RTX 5090s: two GPUs at 4.8B and four at 9.6B. At 9.6B, each of our four 32-GB GPUs holds one large Chorus n-gram table, whose update requires large temporary buffers. sections.title: D Limitations
sections.content: We tested dense models with at most 133M backbone parameters; larger models and other architectures remain untested. The gains on downstream tasks appear to concentrate on natural-language prediction and knowledge recall, rather than reasoning tasks.
